https://b.jlel.se/s/8fb Share online Share this post × Use your browser's share dialog Copy share text I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit. I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me. Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that. Less friction Most of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project. Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort. In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me. Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality. What you lose when you delete ~/.cache

I saved an OpenAI key in
Langflow , stopped it, deleted
~/.cache
and started it again. The key was still in Langflow's database. Langflow just couldn't read it any more, and every time it tried, its log said "API key decryption failed after retry. This may indicate a corrupted key or SECRET_KEY mismatch."
If you install Langflow with pip or uv and don't set anything, the key it encrypts your saved credentials with lives in
~/.cache/langflow/secret_key . Delete that and Langflow makes a new one on the next start, and every API key you saved in it is now noise. You'd have to paste each one back in. Langflow knows the key matters, it even ships a
script
for changing it safely. It just keeps it in the cache.
Which feels a bit unfair, because deleting
~/.cache
is the one bit of tidying everyone agrees is fine. The
XDG spec
says it's for "non-essential data files". The top answer on askubuntu's
Is it okay to delete the ~/.cache folder? , which has been read over half a million times, says "IMO you can delete all of .cache with no long term detrimental effects". Mine's 8.9 GB, 6.4 of it uv's, so I get the temptation.

What you lose when you delete ~/.cache
# ai
# opensource
# linux
# backups
I saved an OpenAI key in
Langflow , stopped it, deleted
~/.cache
and started it again. The key was still in Langflow's database. Langflow just couldn't read it any more, and every time it tried, its log said "API key decryption failed after retry. This may indicate a corrupted key or SECRET_KEY mismatch."
If you install Langflow with pip or uv and don't set anything, the key it encrypts your saved credentials with lives in
~/.cache/langflow/secret_key . Delete that and Langflow makes a new one on the next start, and every API key you saved in it is now noise. You'd have to paste each one back in. Langflow knows the key matters, it even ships a
script
for changing it safely. It just keeps it in the cache.
Which feels a bit unfair, because deleting
~/.cache
is the one bit of tidying everyone agrees is fine. The
XDG spec
says it's for "non-essential data files". The top answer on askubuntu's
Is it okay to delete the ~/.cache folder? , which has been read over half a million times, says "IMO you can delete all of .cache with no long term detrimental effects". Mine's 8.9 GB, 6.4 of it uv's, so I get the temptation.
Somebody did ask askubuntu, back in 2019,
"Is there anything in ~/.cache that is not really cache?"
It's still got no answers, so here's mine.

final_briefs.title: rustyfiles

The README shows a folder of 100 000 files opening in 281 ms, and the project ships binaries for Windows 11 (x64 | ARM64) and macOS 26 on Apple silicon (beta).

final_briefs.description: **A practical workaround shows that a persistent 403 when sharing transcripts in Claude Code is an account‑side issue, not a local bug.** The suggested steps are to re‑run `/login` to confirm a fresh session; if the 403 remains, treat it as an Anthropic account/permission problem and copy the transcript manually as a temporary solution.

final_briefs.description: **Understanding the difference between OCR and ICR helps you choose the right engine for passport data extraction in onboarding pipelines.** OCR converts printed text (including the MRZ) into machine‑readable characters, while ICR is designed for handwriting and more variable styles. The guide walks through the typical OCR workflow—capture, preprocess, recognize, structure—and explains where ICR might be needed.
final_briefs.why_it_matters: Clarifies the trade‑offs between OCR and ICR for passport data extraction, guiding engineers to pick the right technology for identity‑verification pipelines.
final_briefs.who_cares: Engineers building digital onboarding, KYC, or any document‑processing system that must read passports or similar IDs.
